subject: parasitology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch11_color_plates/plate_13.jpg]]
Plate 13 is a fecal specimen seen under 400× using brightfield microscopy. The plate shows the ovum of which parasite?
explanation:
The ova of T.trichiura are brown and shaped like a football, with mucous plugs at both ends. Ova have a thick wall and measure about 50 μm long by 20 μm wide. Enterobius ova are approximately the same size but have a clear (hyaline) shell, are flat on one side, and have a visible larva within. Necator eggs are larger (approximately 65–75 μm long by 40 μm wide) and have a clear shell.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 11 Photomicrographs and Color Plate Examination; section 11; book question 13. Topic path: Microbiology/Identify microscopic morphology/Parasites/2. Color plate attachment included.

subject: parasitology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch11_color_plates/plate_14.jpg]]
Plate 14 is a fecal specimen unstained seen under 400× using brightfield microscopy. The plate shows the ovum of which parasite?
explanation:
Ascaris ova are large and oval, usually measuring 50 to 75 μm long by 35 to 50 μm wide. They are often bile stained and may have a thick shell with a coarse covering (corticated). This egg demonstrates a contracted embryo, leaving space between the shell and the embryo at the opposing poles. This indicates that the egg is fertilized.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 11 Photomicrographs and Color Plate Examination; section 11; book question 14. Topic path: Microbiology/Identify microscopic morphology/Parasites/2. Color plate attachment included.

subject: parasitology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch11_color_plates/plate_15.jpg]]
Plate 15 is an iodine-stained fecal specimen seen under 400× using brightfield microscopy. The plate shows the ovum of which parasite?
explanation:
Hookworm ova are approximately 60 to 75 μm in length and 35 to 40 μm in width. They have a thin outer shell, usually containing an unembryonated or partly embryonated egg within. The ova of Necator and Ancylostoma cannot be differentiated from one another. Threadworm (Strongyloides) produces similar ova, but these hatch in the intestine, releasing the rhabditoid larvae that are found in feces. Pinworm (Enterobius) ova are approximately the same size but are more elongated and flat on one side. Whipworm (Trichuris) ova are smaller and thick walled, with mucous plugs at both ends.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 11 Photomicrographs and Color Plate Examination; section 11; book question 15. Topic path: Microbiology/Identify microscopic morphology/Parasites/2. Color plate attachment included.

subject: parasitology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch11_color_plates/plate_16.jpg]]
Plate 16 is an unstained fecal specimen seen under 400× using brightfield microscopy. The plate shows the ovum of which parasite?
explanation:
C. sinensis produces small, bile-stained ova approximately 25 to 35 μm in length and 10 to 20 μm in width. Ova have a collar (shoulder) on both sides of the operculum and a knob at the end opposite the operculum. Fasciola, Paragonimus, and Fasciolopsis all produce large, yellow-brown operculated ova.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 11 Photomicrographs and Color Plate Examination; section 11; book question 16. Topic path: Microbiology/Identify microscopic morphology/Parasites/2. Color plate attachment included.

subject: parasitology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch11_color_plates/plate_17.jpg]]
Plate 17 is an unstained fecal specimen seen under 400× using brightfield microscopy. The plate shows the ovum of which parasite?
explanation:
P. westermani produces large, operculated ova measuring approximately 80 to 100 μm in length and 50 to 70 μm in width. They are yellow-brown and nonembryonated. Metagonimus and Opisthorchis ova are small ova resembling Clonorchis. Fasciola produces ova that are also yellow-brown, operculated, and unembryonated. The ova are larger than Paragonimus and lack the small shoulders adjacent to the operculum of Paragonimus ova.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 11 Photomicrographs and Color Plate Examination; section 11; book question 17. Topic path: Microbiology/Identify microscopic morphology/Parasites/2. Color plate attachment included.

subject: parasitology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch11_color_plates/plate_19.jpg]]
Plate 19 shows an organism isolated from an eye wash from a patient who had a corneal infection and had been wearing contact lenses for the past 2 years. What is the name of the causative agent?
explanation:
This is a large trophozoite with spiculated cytoplasm characteristic of Acanthamoeba. Eye infections caused by this organism have been documented in contact lens wearers who do not disinfect lenses properly. Acanthamoeba spp. are large trophozoites measuring 25 to 50 μm. They may also cause primary amoebic meningoencephalitis, although they are isolated less often than Naegleria in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of patients with this disease.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 11 Photomicrographs and Color Plate Examination; section 11; book question 19. Topic path: Microbiology/Identify microscopic morphology/Parasites/2. Color plate attachment included.

subject: parasitology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch11_color_plates/plate_20.jpg]]
Plate 20 is a Wright-stained peripheral blood film, 1,000×. Which malarial stage is present in the red blood cell (RBC) in the center of the plate?
option_d: Mature gametocyte stage of Plasmodium ovale
explanation:
The infected RBC demonstrates enlarged ameba-like cytoplasm and Schüffner dots, which are characteristic of P. vivax and P. ovale. The parasite is at the ring-form trophozoite stage.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 11 Photomicrographs and Color Plate Examination; section 11; book question 20. Topic path: Microbiology/Identify microscopic morphology/Parasites/3. Color plate attachment included.

subject: parasitology
question:
[[media:assets/question-media/harr_ch11_color_plates/plate_21.jpg]]
Plate 21 is a modified acid-fast stain with malachite green counterstain of a stool specimen, 1,000× magnification. The oocysts seen in this field are approximately 5 µm in diameter. Which organism is present?
explanation:
All of the organisms listed are coccidian parasites that cause diarrhea, especially in patients with immunodeficiency (e.g., those with AIDS). Cryptosporidium produces the smallest oocysts (half the size of Cyclospora, which is the next smallest) and is visible in stools with use of either acid-fast or immunofluorescent staining techniques. The oocysts are round, about 5 μm in diameter, and stain deep pink.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); Chapter 11 Photomicrographs and Color Plate Examination; section 11; book question 21. Topic path: Microbiology/Identify microscopic morphology/Parasites/2. Color plate attachment included.

subject: parasitology
question: Parasitic organisms that may be transmitted sexually do not include:
explanation:
Of the organisms listed, Diphyllobothrium latum cannot be transmitted sexually; this infection is acquired from the ingestion of infected raw or poorly cooked freshwater fish.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 4; continuous question 389. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and epidemiology/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: The incorrect match between organism and the appropriate diagnostic procedure is:
option_c: Enterobius vermicularis—routine ova and parasite examination
explanation:
The appropriate procedure for the diagnosis of E. vermicularis would involve the microscopic examination of a series of consecutive cellulose tapes. Typical eggs and/or a rare adult pinworm could be identified under the microscope.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 1; continuous question 386. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic techniques/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
Charcot-Leyden crystals in stool may be associated with an immune response and are
thought to be formed from the breakdown products of:
explanation:
When eosinophils disintegrate, the granules reform into Charcot-Leyden crystals.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 3; continuous question 388. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of the morphology of artifacts/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question:
Gram staining of a sample from a gum lesion showed what appeared to be amoebae. A
trichrome smear showed amoebae with a single nucleus and partially digested PMNs.
The correct identification is:
explanation:
E. gingivalis is known to be an inhabitant of the mouth and is characterized by morphology that resembles E. histolytica/E. dispar. However, E. gingivalis tends to ingest PMNs, whereas E. histolytica/E. dispar do not.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 10; continuous question 395. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology and body site/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
Patients with severe diarrhea should use “enteric precautions” to prevent nosocomial
infections with:
explanation:
Cryptosporidium oocysts (unlike those of C. belli) are immediately infective when passed in stool, and nosocomial infections have been well documented with this coccidian.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 58; continuous question 443. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and life cycles/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
In a condition resulting from the accidental ingestion of eggs, the human becomes the
intermediate host, rather than the definitive host. The correct answer is:
explanation:
The accidental ingestion of T. solium eggs can result in the disease called cysticercosis. The cysticerci will develop in a number of different tissues, including the brain, and humans are accidental intermediate hosts.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 55; continuous question 440. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and life cycles/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
A transplant recipient on immunosuppressive drugs developed increasing diarrhea.
The most likely combination of disease and diagnostic procedure is:
explanation:
The fact that the patient has received a transplant, is on immunosuppressive drugs, and has increasing diarrhea, suggests infection with microsporidia; the most appropriate method would be the modified trichrome stain.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 56; continuous question 441. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
After returning from a 2-year stay in India, a patient has eosinophilia, an enlarged left
spermatic cord, and bilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy. The most likely clinical
specimen and organism match is:
option_b: Urine and concentration for Trichomonas vaginalis
explanation:
On the basis of the history, the most relevant procedure to perform is the preparation and examination of thick blood films for the recovery and identification of microfilariae. The symptoms suggest early filariasis.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 57; continuous question 442. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: Key characteristics of infection with Plasmodium knowlesi include:
option_a: Rapid erythrocyte cycle (24 hours), will infect all ages of RBCs, and can cause serious disease
option_b: Erythrocytic cycle limited to young RBCs and causes a relatively benign disease
option_c: The possibility of a true relapse from the liver, infection in older RBCs, and causes serious disease
option_d: Extended life cycle (72 hours), will infect all ages of RBCs, and disease is similar to that caused by Plasmodium ovale.
explanation:
Characteristics of the fifth human malaria, P. knowlesi, include a rapid erythrocytic cycle of 24 hours, possible infection of all ages of RBCs (as with P. falciparum), and the potential for serious disease (as with P. falciparum).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 76; continuous question 461. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and pathogenesis/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
Autofluorescence requires no stain and is recommended for the presumptive
identification of:
explanation:
Autofluorescence is often used in preliminary testing for the presence of C. cayetanensis oocysts (8–10 μm). If positive, then the specimen can be stained using modified acid-fast stains for confirmation.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 75; continuous question 460. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: Key characteristics of the thick film include:
option_a: The ability to see the parasite within the RBCs
option_b: The ability to identify the parasites to the species level
option_c: The examination of less blood than the thin blood film
option_d: The necessity to lake the RBCs during or prior to staining
explanation:
With thick blood films, the RBCs must be ruptured/laked either prior to or during staining. Without laking the RBCs, the stained smears would be too thick or too dark to be able to visualize any morphology. In contrast, the thin blood film is fixed prior to/during staining to preserve the RBC morphology; the parasite morphology within the infected RBC can be reviewed for possible diagnosis to the species level. The thin film has a much smaller amount of blood than the thick blood film.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 80; continuous question 465. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of specimen processing and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2 Answer to Question 80.

subject: parasitology
question:
Although a patient is strongly suspected of having giardiasis and is still symptomatic,
three routine stool examinations (O&P examination) have been performed correctly
and reported as negative. Biopsy confirmed the patient had giardiasis. Reasons for
these findings may include:
option_a: The patient was coinfected with several bacterial species
option_b: Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis) tends to adhere to the mucosal surface and more than three stool examinations may be required to confirm a suspected infection
option_c: The organisms present did not stain with trichrome stain, and therefore the morphology is very atypical
option_d: Special diagnostic procedures, such as the Knott concentration and nutrient-free agar cultures, should have been used
explanation:
It is well known that G. lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis) trophozoites adhere to the intestinal mucosal surface by means of the sucking disk. Although a patient may have giardiasis and be symptomatic, confirmation of the infection from stool examinations may require more than the routine three stools or may require the examination of duodenal contents. These organisms are shed very sporadically. Two fecal immunoassays may be required to diagnose giardiasis; this also relates to sporadic shedding. The need for two fecal immunoassays does not apply to cryptosporidiosis; a single immunoassay is sufficient.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.12; book question 59; continuous question 524. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles, organism morphology, pathogenesis, and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
A transplant recipient is currently receiving steroids. The patient is now complaining of
abdominal pain and has symptoms of pneumonia and positive blood cultures with
gram-negative rods. The individual has been living in the United States for 20 years but
grew up in Central America. The most likely parasite causing these symptoms is:
explanation:
Although infection with S. stercoralis may have been acquired in Central America many years before, the patient may have remained asymptomatic while the infection was maintained at a low level in the body via the autoinfective portion of the life cycle. As the patient became more immunosuppressed (steroids), the life cycle began to reactivate with penetration of the larvae through the intestinal wall (abdominal pain) and larval migration through the lungs (pneumonia), and the patient may have presented with evidence of sepsis (often with gram-negative bacteria carried with the larvae as they penetrate the intestinal wall). In patients who become immunosuppressed, the life cycle of Strongyloides may be reactivated, and this results in serious illness (e.g., hyperinfection syndrome, disseminated disease); this can occur many years after the initial infection and after the patient has left the endemic area.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.12; book question 60; continuous question 525. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of fundamental life cycles, pathogenesis, and immunosuppressives/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
Visceral larva migrans is associated with which of the following organisms and
diagnostic method?
explanation:
Toxocara spp. are the cause of visceral larva migrans and occur when humans accidentally ingest the infective eggs of the dog or cat ascarid. The larvae migrate through the deep tissues, including the eye. The test of choice is the serology.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 14; continuous question 399. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
The following organisms are linked with specific, relevant information. The incorrect
combination is:
option_d: Balantidium coli—common in the United States
explanation:
B. coli is a ciliate that can cause watery diarrhea in humans; however, it is not commonly found within the United States. It is the largest of the intestinal protozoa and can be found in proficiency testing specimens. Therefore, although it is not common, laboratories must still be able to identify these organisms.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 15; continuous question 400. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle and epidemiology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: The incorrect match between the organism and one method of acquiring the infection is:
option_a: Trypanosoma brucei rhodesiense—bite of sand fleas
option_b: Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis)—ingestion of water contaminated with cysts
option_c: Hookworm—skin penetration of larvae from soil
option_d: Toxoplasma gondii—ingestion of infected raw or rare meats
explanation:
East and West African trypanosomiasis (T. B. rhodesiense and T. B. gambiense) are acquired when infective forms are introduced into the human body through the bite of the tse-tse fly, not sand fleas.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 5; continuous question 390. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of fundamental life cycles/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: Fecal immunoassays have become more commonly used to diagnose infections with:
option_b: Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis) and Cryptosporidium spp.
explanation:
Fecal immunoassays have become more commonly used for the diagnosis of infections with Giardia and Cryptosporidium. These tests are available in EIA, FA, or rapid cartridge formats.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 37; continuous question 422. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: Early ring forms of the fifth human malaria, Plasmodium knowlesi, resemble those of:
explanation:
Early ring forms of the fifth human malaria, P. knowlesi, resemble most closely ring forms of P. falciparum. However, in the early ring form stage, all human malaria species tend to look very similar.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 72; continuous question 457. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
One of the following protozoan organisms has been implicated in waterborne and
foodborne outbreaks within the United States. The suspect organism is:
explanation:
For a number of years, G. lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis) has been implicated in both waterborne and foodborne outbreaks from the ingestion of infective cysts within contaminated water and food.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 9; continuous question 394. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and epidemiology/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question:
The microsporidia are organisms (now classified with the fungi) that have been
implicated in human disease primarily in:
option_d: Patients who have been traveling in the tropics
explanation:
Although the microsporidia have been known as pathogens in many groups of animals, their involvement in humans has primarily been in immunocompromised patients, especially those with AIDS. Microsporidia can be found in different tissues, and currently, there are a number of genera implicated in human disease.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 41; continuous question 426. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and epidemiology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
Although the pathogenicity of Blastocystis spp. remains controversial, newer
information suggests that:
option_a: Most organisms are misdiagnosed as artifacts
option_b: Approximately 10 subtypes/strains are included in the name, some of which are pathogenic and some are nonpathogenic
option_c: The immune status of the host is solely responsible for symptomatic infections
option_d: The number of organisms present determines pathogenicity
explanation:
Although the pathogenicity of Blastocystis spp. continues to be debated (some patients are symptomatic, and some are asymptomatic), it is now known that the organisms we see microscopically comprise a number of subtypes/strains/subspecies. Approximately half these subtypes are pathogenic for humans, and half are nonpathogenic; however, morphologically they all look the same. Correct reporting of this infection should be Blastocystis spp.; numbers should also be reported (rare, few, moderate, many, packed).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 78; continuous question 463. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology and pathogenesis/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: An E. histolytica (true pathogen) trophozoite has the following characteristics:
option_a: Compact karyosome in the nucleus, ingested RBCs, and clear pseudopodia
option_b: Ingested RBCs, clear pseudopodia, and uneven chromatin on the nuclear membrane
option_c: Ingested RBCs, clear pseudopodia, and large glycogen vacuoles in cytoplasm
option_d: Large, blotlike karyosome, ingested white blood cells (WBCs), and granular pseudopods
explanation:
The trophozoite of E. histolytica has evenly arranged chromatin on the nuclear membrane; a central, compact karyosome in the nucleus; clear pseudopodia; and ingested RBCs in the cytoplasm.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 11; continuous question 396. Topic path: Parasitology.

subject: parasitology
question: An operculated cestode egg that can be recovered from human feces is:
explanation:
D. latum is the only operculated cestode egg that is found in humans; the infection is acquired from the ingestion of infected raw or poorly cooked freshwater fish.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 20; continuous question 405. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question:
Organisms that should be considered in a nursery school outbreak of diarrhea
include:
option_a: Endolimax nana, Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis), and Entamoeba coli
option_b: Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis), Dientamoeba fragilis, and Cryptosporidium parvum
option_c: Cryptosporidium spp., Trichomonas vaginalis, and Entamoeba coli
option_d: Trichomonas hominis, Dientamoeba fragilis, and Endolimax nana
explanation:
G. lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis), D. fragilis, and Cryptosporidium have been implicated in nursery school outbreaks. Among the many protozoa and coccidia found in the human, these three organisms have become the most likely parasites in this type of setting.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 31; continuous question 416. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of epidemiology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: In infections with Taenia solium, humans can serve as the:
option_c: Either the definitive or the intermediate host
explanation:
If humans ingest T. solium cysticerci in uncooked or rare pork, the adult tapeworm will mature within the intestine (human will serve as definitive host); if eggs from the adult tapeworm are ingested, then the cysticerci will develop in human tissues (accidental intermediate host), causing cysticercosis.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 22; continuous question 407. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
In a patient with diarrhea, occasionally Entamoeba histolytica/E. dispar (four nucleated
cysts, no chromatoidal bars) are identified as being present; however, these cells, which
are misdiagnosed as protozoa, are really:
explanation:
As PMNs in stool begin to fragment and appear to have four nuclei, they will resemble E. histolytica/E. dispar cysts. However, E. histolytica/E. dispar cysts are rarely seen in cases of diarrhea. The species name E. histolytica is reserved for the true pathogen, whereas E. dispar is used for the nonpathogenic species. Unfortunately, they look identical morphologically. The only time E. histolytica could be identified morphologically would be from trophozoites containing ingested RBCs. Nonpathogenic E. dispar would not contain ingested RBCs. The correct way to report these organisms is E. histolytica/E. dispar (no trophozoites containing ingested RBCs) or E. histolytica (trophozoites seen that contain ingested RBCs). Physicians may base the treatment on patient symptoms.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 2; continuous question 387. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of the morphology of artifacts/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: The term internal autoinfection can be associated with the following parasites:
option_a: Cryptosporidium spp. and Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis)
option_d: Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis) and Cystoisospora belli
explanation:
Both Cryptosporidium and Strongyloides have the capability for internal autoinfection in their life cycles. This means that the cycle and infection can continue even after the patient has left the endemic area. In the case of Cryptosporidium, the cycle continues in patients who are immunocompromised and incapable of self cure.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 68; continuous question 453. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: Oocysts of Cryptosporidium spp. can be detected in stool specimens by using:
explanation:
Oocysts of Cryptosporidium spp. can be found and identified using microscopic examination of fecal smears stained with modified acid-fast stains. They appear as purple-red-pink round objects, measuring approximately 4 to 6 μm. Often the four sporozoites and residual body can be seen within the oocyst wall.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 28; continuous question 413. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic procedures, staining characteristics/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: Confirmation of an infection with microsporidia can be achieved by seeing:
option_d: Organisms stained with modified acid-fast stains
explanation:
Evidence of the cross/diagonal line polar tubules provides confirmation for microsporidial spores in the clinical specimen. Not all spores will contain visible polar tubules; the stain of choice is the modified trichrome stain (Ryan/blue or Weber/green).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 71; continuous question 456. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: Toxoplasma gondii is characterized by:
option_a: Possible congenital infection and ingestion of oocysts
option_b: Cosmopolitan distribution and possible difficulties with interpretation of serological results
explanation:
Infection with T. gondii is acquired through the ingestion of infected rare or raw meats, infective oocysts from cat feces, or as a congenital transmission. The organism has a cosmopolitan distribution and although serological testing is generally the test of choice, the results may be very difficult to interpret in certain situations (e.g., congenital infection and immunocompromised patients).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 27; continuous question 412. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of all areas of parasite biology, diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
Protozoan cysts were seen in a concentration sediment and tentatively identified as
Entamoeba coli. However, the organisms were barely visible on the permanent stained
smear because:
option_a: The organisms were actually not present in the concentration sediment
option_b: There were too few cysts to allow identification on the stained smear
option_c: Entamoeba coli cysts were present but poorly fixed due to the thick cyst wall
option_d: The concentrate and permanent stained smear were not from the same patient
explanation:
As E. coli cysts mature, the cyst wall becomes more impenetrable to fixatives. Consequently, the cysts may be visible in the concentrate sediment but appear very distorted or pale on the permanent stained smear.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 52; continuous question 437. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of fixatives and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: The most prevalent helminth to infect humans is:
option_b: Ascaris lumbricoides, the large intestinal roundworm
option_d: Schistosoma mansoni, one of the blood flukes
explanation:
The pinworm, E. vermicularis, is the most common parasitic infection throughout the world, and the eggs are infective within just a few hours. It has been said, “You either had the infection as a child, have it now, or will have it again when you have children.”

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 64; continuous question 449. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and epidemiology/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question:
A 60-year-old Brazilian patient with cardiac irregularities and congestive heart failure
suddenly dies. Examination of the myocardium revealed numerous amastigotes, an
indication that the cause of death was most likely:
explanation:
T. cruzi, the cause of Chagas disease, exists in two forms within humans, the trypomastigote in the blood and the amastigote in the striated muscle (usually cardiac muscle and intestinal tract muscle).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 59; continuous question 444. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and life cycles/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
In an outbreak of diarrheal disease traced to a municipal water supply, the most likely
causative agent is:
explanation:
Cryptosporidium can be transmitted through contaminated municipal water sources. Such outbreaks have been well documented.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 61; continuous question 446. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and epidemiology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
When analysis of blood smears for malaria are requested, what patient information
should be obtained?
option_c: Travel history, antimalarial medication, date of return to United States
explanation:
Travel history (areas of drug resistance), the date of return to the United States (primary versus relapse case), and history of antimalarial medication and illness (severe illness, few organisms on smear) are very important questions to ask. Without this information, a malaria diagnosis can be missed or delayed with severe patient consequences.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 60; continuous question 445. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and life cycle, and epidemiology/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: Which of the following statements is true regarding onchocerciasis?
option_a: The adult worm is present in blood
option_b: The microfilariae are in blood during the late evening hours
option_c: The diagnostic test of choice is the skin snip
option_d: The parasite resides in the deep lymphatics
explanation:
The adult O. volvulus reside in subcutaneous nodules, and the microfilariae are found in the fluids right under the outer layers of skin; thus the appropriate diagnostic test is the microscopic examination of skin snips for the presence of microfilariae.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 63; continuous question 448. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
Within the United States, sporadic mini-outbreaks of diarrheal disease have been
associated with the ingestion of strawberries, raspberries, fresh basil, mesclun (baby
lettuce leaves), and snow peas. The most likely causative agent is:
explanation:
The coccidian C. cayetanensis has been linked to mini-outbreaks of diarrheal disease. Epidemiological evidence strongly implicates various berries, basil, mesclun, and snow peas as likely causes. These outbreaks are very sporadic and tend to occur primarily in March through May, primarily from imported foods.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 62; continuous question 447. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and epidemiology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: A helminth egg is described as having terminal polar plugs. The most likely helminth is:
explanation:
The eggs of T. trichiura (the whipworm) have been described as being barrel shaped, with a thick shell and two polar plugs, one at each end of the egg.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 65; continuous question 450. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: Ingestion of which of the following eggs will result in infection?
explanation:
The eggs of T. canis are infectious for humans and cause visceral and ocular larva migrans. These ascarid eggs of the dog can infect humans; the eggs hatch and the larvae wander through the deep tissues, occasionally the eye. In this case, the human becomes the accidental intermediate host.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 66; continuous question 451. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: Plasmodium vivax and Plasmodium ovale are similar because they:
option_a: Exhibit Schüffner dots and have a true relapse in the life cycle
option_b: Have no malarial pigment and multiple rings
option_c: Commonly have appliqué forms in the red cells
option_d: Have true stippling, do not have a relapse stage, and infect old red cells
explanation:
Both P. vivax and P. ovale infect young RBCs, have true stippling (Schüffner dots), contain malarial pigment, and have a true relapse stage in the life cycle.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 67; continuous question 452. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and morphology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
Older developing stages (trophozoites, schizonts) of the fifth human malaria,
Plasmodium knowlesi, resemble those of:
explanation:
Older developing stages (developing trophozoites, schizonts) of the fifth human malaria, P. knowlesi, tend to closely resemble those of P. malariae (band forms, “daisy head” mature schizont).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 74; continuous question 459. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
Microsporidia have been identified as causing severe diarrhea, disseminated disease in
other body sites, and ocular infections. Routes of infection have been identified as:
option_d: Ingestion, inhalation, and direct contamination from the environment
explanation:
Infectious routes for microsporidial infections have been confirmed as ingestion and inhalation of the spores; direct transfer of infectious spores from environmental surfaces to the eyes has also been reported.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 69; continuous question 454. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: Microsporidial infections can be confirmed by using:
option_a: Light microscopy and modified trichrome staining
option_b: Phase contrast microscopy and routine trichrome staining
option_c: Electron microscopy and modified acid-fast staining
explanation:
The use of a modified trichrome stain (Ryan/blue, Weber/green; both with a very high dye content) and light microscopy (oil immersion using the 100× objective) can be used to confirm a microsporidial infection.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 77; continuous question 462. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
An immunocompromised patient continues to have diarrhea after repeated ova and
parasites (O&P) examinations (sedimentation concentration, trichrome permanent
stained smear) were reported as negative; organisms that might be responsible for the
diarrhea include:
option_a: Cryptosporidium spp., Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis), and Cystoisospora belli
option_b: Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis), microsporidia, and Endolimax nana
explanation:
Routine O&P examinations usually do not allow the detection of Cryptosporidium oocysts and microsporidial spores; special stains are required. Modified acid-fast stains for Cryptosporidium and modified trichrome stains for the microsporidia are recommended.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 70; continuous question 455. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
Parasite stages that are immediately infective for humans on passage from the
gastrointestinal tract include:
explanation:
On passage in stool from the gastrointestinal tract, the oocysts of Cryptosporidium are immediately infective; nosocomial infections have been documented with this organism. The oocysts of other coccidia have to undergo further development before they are infective.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 73; continuous question 458. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and organism morphology/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
Potential problems using EDTA anticoagulant and holding the blood too long prior to
preparation of thick and thin blood films include:
option_a: Changes in parasite morphology, loss of organisms within several hours, and poor staining
option_b: Loss of Schüffner dots, poor adherence of the blood to the glass slide, and parasites beginning the vector cycle within the tube of blood
explanation:
All of the changes mentioned are seen in a tube of EDTA blood that has been held too long prior to blood film preparation. Many morphological changes of the parasites, as well as lost organisms, occur under these conditions. These blood specimens should always be handled STAT (ordering, collection, processing, examination, and reporting).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 79; continuous question 464. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of specimen collection and processing, organism morphology, and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
A patient has been diagnosed as having amebiasis but continues to be asymptomatic.
The physician has asked for an explanation and recommendations regarding follow-up.
Suggestions should include:
option_a: Consideration of Entamoeba histolytica versus Entamoeba dispar
option_b: A request for an additional three stools for culture
option_c: Initiating therapy, regardless of the patient’s asymptomatic status
explanation:
It is now well established that E. histolytica is being used to designate the true pathogenic species, whereas E. dispar is now being used to designate nonpathogenic species. Unless trophozoites containing ingested RBCs (E. histolytica) are seen, the two organisms cannot be differentiated on the basis of morphology. On the basis of this information, there are now two separate species, only one of which (E. histolytica) is pathogenic. Because this patient is asymptomatic, the organisms seen in the fecal smears are probably E. dispar (nonpathogen); the laboratory report should have said “Entamoeba histolytica/Entamoeba dispar”—unable to differentiate on the basis of morphology unless trophozoites are seen to contain ingested RBCs (E. histolytica— true pathogen). Immunoassays and real time PCR can differentiate the true pathogen, E. histolytica, from nonpathogenic species of Entamoeba, and are more sensitive and specific than microscopic examination alone.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.12; book question 58; continuous question 523. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of the morphology of organisms and pathogenesis/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
A patient is being seen in the emergency room for a low-grade fever, headache, and
general malaise after returning from a photographic safari in Africa. The physician has
requested blood analysis for malaria; the laboratory would like to have patient
information regarding:
option_a: Specific travel history and body temperature every 4 hours
option_b: Liver function tests and prophylactic medication history
option_c: Transfusion history and body temperature every 4 hours
option_d: Prophylactic medication history and specific travel history
explanation:
If the patient has malaria and has been taking prophylaxis (often sporadically), the number of parasites on the blood smear will be reduced and examination of routine thick and thin blood films should be more exhaustive. Furthermore, specific geographic travel history may help to determine whether chloroquine-resistant P. falciparum may be a factor. Also, if the patient is immunologically naïve (no prior exposure to malaria), these patients usually come into an emergency room with a very low parasitemia and no periodicity; thus malaria may not even be suspected.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.12; book question 56; continuous question 521. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles, diagnostic techniques, and clinical presentation/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
Examination of a modified acid-fast–stained fecal smear reveals round structures
measuring approximately 8 to 10 µm, some of which are stained and some of which are
not. They do not appear to show any internal morphology. The patient is symptomatic
with diarrhea, and the cause may be:
explanation:
One of the coccidian parasites, C. cayetanensis, has been implicated in cases of human diarrhea. The recommended stains are modified acid-fast stains, and the organisms are quite variable in their staining characteristics. The color can range from clear (resembling wrinkled cellophane) to red-purple. The oocysts are immature when passed (no internal morphology) and they measure about 8 to 10 μm.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.12; book question 57; continuous question 522. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of the morphology of artifacts, organism life cycles, and diagnostic methods/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: Which of the following is the best technique to identify Dientamoeba fragilis in stool?
explanation:
The best technique to recover and identify D. fragilis trophozoites and rare cysts would be the trichrome-stained smear.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 8; continuous question 393. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: Upon examination of stool material for Cystoisospora belli, one would expect to see:
option_c: Oocysts that are modified acid-fast positive
explanation:
C. belli oocysts in various stages of maturity would be seen in the concentrate sediment or possibly the direct, wet preparation; these oocysts would stain positive with modified acid-fast stains.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 6; continuous question 391. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles and organism morphology/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: Which specimen is the least likely to provide recovery of Trichomonas vaginalis?
explanation:
T. vaginalis is site-specific. The organisms are found in the urogenital tract; thus, the intestinal tract is not the normal site for these organisms.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 7; continuous question 392. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
Characteristics of the rhabditiform (noninfective) larvae of Strongyloides stercoralis
include a:
option_a: Short buccal capsule and large genital primordium
option_b: Long buccal capsule and pointed tail
option_c: Short buccal capsule and small genital primordium
option_d: Small genital primordium and notch in tail
explanation:
The rhabditiform larvae of S. stercoralis are characterized by the short buccal capsule (mouth) and large genital primordium, whereas hookworm larvae have a long buccal capsule and very small genital primordium.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 13; continuous question 398. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology and life cycle/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
A 12-year-old girl is brought to the emergency room with meningitis and a history of
swimming in a warm-water spring. Motile amoebae that measure 10 μm in size are seen
in CSF and are most likely:
explanation:
N. fowleri are free-living soil and water amoebae that cause primary amebic meningoencephalitis (PAM). The number of cases reported is few; however, the infection is very acute and almost always fatal.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 12; continuous question 397. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle and epidemiology/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: The incorrect match between symptoms and disease is:
option_c: Cardiac involvement and chronic Chagas disease
explanation:
T. trichiura (whipworm) may cause diarrhea and occasionally dysentery in very heavy infections; however, the worms are confined to the intestine, and myalgias are not seen in this helminth infection.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 43; continuous question 428. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle and pathogenesis/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
Examination of 24-hour unpreserved urine specimen is sometimes helpful in the
recovery of:
explanation:
S. haematobium blood flukes reside in the veins over the bladder. When the eggs are passed from the body, they are often found in urine; egg viability can also be determined in unpreserved urine.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 16; continuous question 401. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle and diagnostic methods/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: Eating poorly cooked infected pork can lead to an infection with:
explanation:
Both T. solium (pork tapeworm) and T. spiralis can be acquired from the ingestion of raw or poorly cooked infected pork.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 19; continuous question 404. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism life cycle/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: Two helminth eggs that may resemble one another are:
explanation:
Both D. latum and P. westermani eggs are operculated and approximately the same size. The morphology is similar, although D. latum has a knob at the abopercular end and P. westermani has a thickened abopercular end and shoulders into which the operculum fits.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 18; continuous question 403. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of organism morphology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: The examination of sputum may be necessary to diagnose infection with:
explanation:
P. westermani adult worms are found in the lung, and eggs may be coughed up in the sputum. Consequently, both sputum and stool (if the sputum containing the eggs is swallowed) are the recommended specimens for examination for the eggs.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 17; continuous question 402. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle and diagnostic methods/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: The adult tapeworm of Echinococcus granulosus is found in the intestine of:
explanation:
Although hydatid cysts are found in sheep or in humans (accidental intermediate host), the adult tapeworms of E. granulosus are found in the intestine of the dog.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 21; continuous question 406. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: The incorrect match between method and method objective is:
option_a: Direct wet examination and detection of organism motility
option_b: Knott concentration and the recovery of operculated helminth eggs
option_c: Baermann concentration and the recovery of Strongyloides
option_d: Permanent stained fecal smear and confirmation of protozoa
explanation:
The Knott concentration is designed to allow the recovery of microfilariae from a blood specimen. Dilute formalin (2%) is used; blood is introduced into the formalin, the red cells lyse, and the sediment can be examined as a wet preparation or permanent stained smear (Giemsa or hematoxylin-based stain) for the presence of microfilariae.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 45; continuous question 430. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: The incorrect match between organism and characteristic/diagnostic method is:
option_a: Dientamoeba fragilis and tetrad karyosome in the nucleus
option_d: Schistosoma mansoni and egg with terminal spine
explanation:
The egg of S. mansoni is characterized by a large lateral spine; S. haematobium has the characteristic terminal spine.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 46; continuous question 431. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of morphology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
Organisms (and infections) that under normal conditions cannot be transmitted in the
laboratory are:
explanation:
A. lumbricoides eggs require a period of development in the soil before they are infective for humans. The other organisms listed can be transmitted within the laboratory or in the hospital setting.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 26; continuous question 411. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: Which microfilariae are usually not found circulating in peripheral blood?
explanation:
O. volvulus microfilariae are normally found in the fluid right under the outer layer of skin. Therefore, the skin snip is the proper specimen to examine.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 29; continuous question 414. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic procedures, staining characteristics/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question: Humans acquire infections with Diphyllobothrium latum adult worms by:
explanation:
The ingestion of raw freshwater fish containing the encysted larvae of D. latum will result in the development of an adult tapeworm within the human intestine.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 23; continuous question 408. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question:
Babesia is an organism that has been implicated in disease from both splenectomized
and nonsplenectomized patients. Morphologically, the parasites resemble:
explanation:
Babesia is an intracellular parasite that closely resembles the ring forms (early trophozoites) of P. falciparum. Often in babesiosis there are more rings per cell and the ring form is the only stage seen.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 25; continuous question 410. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of parasite morphology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: Humans can serve as both the intermediate and definitive host in infections caused by:
explanation:
In infections with H. nana, humans serve as both intermediate and definitive hosts. When ingested, the oncosphere penetrates the intestinal mucosa, develops into the mature cysticercoid (human is intermediate host), and returns to the gut, where the adult tapeworm matures (human is definitive host). Thus, the life cycle can go from egg to adult tapeworm within the human host.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 24; continuous question 409. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycle/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question:
There are few procedures considered STAT in parasitology. The most obvious situation
would be:
option_a: Ova and parasite examination for giardiasis
explanation:
The request for blood films for malaria should always be considered a STAT request. Any laboratory providing these services should have coverage 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. In cases of P. falciparum malaria, any delay in diagnosing the infection could be fatal for the patient.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 47; continuous question 432. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question:
Massive hemolysis, blackwater fever, and central nervous system involvement are most
common with:
explanation:
The pathogenic sequelae of malarial infections with P. falciparum are the most severe of the four species listed. They can include massive hemolysis, blackwater fever, and multiple organ involvement, including the central nervous system (cerebral malaria).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 30; continuous question 415. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of disease pathogenesis/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: The miracidial hatching test helps to demonstrate the viability of eggs of:
explanation:
The determination of egg viability is important in schistosomiasis; therefore, the miracidial hatching test is helpful in demonstrating the egg viability of Schistosoma species. Once the eggs are hatched, the living miracidium larvae will be visible in the water.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 35; continuous question 420. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question:
Organisms that should be considered in a waterborne outbreak of diarrheal disease
include:
option_a: Giardia lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis) and Cryptosporidium spp.
explanation:
Both G. lamblia (G. intestinalis, G. duodenalis) and Cryptosporidium have been implicated in waterborne outbreaks or diarrheal disease. These infections would result from the ingestion of Giardia cysts and/or Cryptosporidium oocysts.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 36; continuous question 421. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of epidemiology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: The incorrect match between disease and symptoms is:
option_c: Toxoplasmosis in compromised host—central nervous system symptoms
explanation:
Infections with E. vermicularis (the pinworm) may cause anal itching, sleeplessness, and possibly some vaginal irritation or discharge; however, dysentery (bloody diarrhea) has not been associated with this infection.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 32; continuous question 417. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: Cysts of Iodamoeba bütschlii typically have:
option_d: Many ingested bacteria and yeast cells
explanation:
The cyst of I. bütschlii is characterized by a large glycogen vacuole that is seen on the wet smear (stains brown with iodine) and on the permanent stained smear (vacuole will appear clear). Occasionally the vacuole will be so large that the organism will collapse on itself.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 34; continuous question 419. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of morphology/Parasitology/1.

subject: parasitology
question:
The formalin-ether (ethyl acetate) concentration procedure for feces is used to
demonstrate:
explanation:
The ova and parasite examination contains three components: the direct wet film (demonstrates protozoan trophozoite motility), the formalin-ethyl acetate concentration (demonstrates protozoan cysts, coccidian oocysts, and helminth eggs), and the trichrome or iron hematoxylin–stained smear (confirms protozoan cysts and trophozoites).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 33; continuous question 418. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
An immunosuppressed man has several episodes of pneumonia, intestinal pain, sepsis
with gram-negative rods, and a history of military service in Southeast Asia 20 years
earlier. The most likely cause is infection with:
explanation:
A latent infection with S. stercoralis acquired years before may cause severe symptoms in the immunosuppressed patient (“autoinfective” capability of life cycle and migratory route through the body leading to the hyperinfection syndrome and disseminated disease).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 48; continuous question 433. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and life cycles/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: Eye infections with Acanthamoeba spp. have most commonly been traced to:
option_c: Use of contaminated lens care solutions
option_d: Failure to remove lenses while swimming
explanation:
The majority of eye infections with Acanthamoeba spp. have resulted from the use of contaminated eye care solutions, primarily the use of homemade saline. It is recommended that all solutions be discarded at the expiration date. Continued use may increase the risk of environmental contamination of the fluids.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 39; continuous question 424. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of epidemiology/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
Select the most sensitive recovery method for Acanthamoeba spp. from lens care
solutions or corneal biopsies.
option_b: The use of monoclonal reagents for the detection of antibody
option_c: The use of non-nutrient agar cultures seeded with Escherichia coli
explanation:
Currently, the most sensitive method of those listed for the recovery of Acanthamoeba spp. from clinical specimens is the non-nutrient agar culture plate seeded with E. coli. The amoebae feed on the bacteria; both trophozoites and cysts can be recovered from the agar surface.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 40; continuous question 425. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: The most common infections with the microsporidia often originate in:
explanation:
With the possible exception of direct inoculation infection in the eye, the microsporidia are thought to initially infect the gastrointestinal (GI) tract through ingestion of the infective spores; infections in other body sites are thought to disseminate from the GI tract.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 38; continuous question 423. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
When staining Cystoisospora belli oocysts with modified acid-fast stains, the important
difference between these methods and the acid-fast stains used for acid-fast bacilli
(AFB) is:
option_a: The staining time is much longer with regular AFB acid-fast stains.
option_b: The decolorizer is much weaker than acid alcohol used for AFB decolorizing.
option_c: A counterstain must be used for the modified methods.
option_d: The stain is more concentrated when staining for AFB.
explanation:
The decolorizer in modified acid-fast stains (Kinyoun cold method, modified hot method) is usually 1% to 3% sulfuric acid rather than the much stronger acid alcohol used in the routine AFB stains.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 42; continuous question 427. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
A 45-year-old hunter developed fever, myalgia, and periorbital edema. He has a history
of bear meat consumption. The most likely causative agent is:
explanation:
Bear meat is another excellent source of T. spiralis. In this case, the patient had evidently consumed poorly cooked infected bear meat, thus ingesting the encysted larvae of T. spiralis.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 54; continuous question 439. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and life cycles/Parasitology/3.

subject: parasitology
question: The incorrect match between organism and characteristic is:
option_a: Chilomastix mesnili and Shepherd’s crook and lemon shape
explanation:

explanation:

subject: parasitology
question:
Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is a form of larva migrans, causing fever,
headache, stiff neck, and increased cells in the spinal fluid. It is caused by:
explanation:
Eosinophilic meningoencephalitis is a form of larva migrans and is caused by A. cantonensis, the rat lungworm. This infection, common in the Pacific region, is associated with CSF symptoms and sometimes eye involvement.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 50; continuous question 435. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of pathogenesis and life cycle/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question:
“Cultures of parasites are different from bacterial cultures; no quality control is
needed.” This statement is:
option_a: True, if two tubes of media are set up for each patient
option_b: True, if the media are checked every 24 hours
option_c: False, unless two different types of media are used
option_d: False, and organism and media controls need to be set up
explanation:
Duplicate cultures should be set up, and specific American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) strains should be cultured along with the patient specimens to confirm that the culture system is operating properly. This approach is somewhat different from that used in diagnostic bacteriology and mycology.

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 51; continuous question 436. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of diagnostic procedures/Parasitology/2.

subject: parasitology
question: When humans have hydatid disease, the causative agent and host classification are:
explanation:
The cause of hydatid disease is E. granulosus, and the human is classified as the accidental intermediate host. Infection occurs when humans accidentally ingest the eggs of E. granulosus and the hydatid cysts develop in the liver, lung, and other organs of the human instead of sheep (normal cycle).

Source: Medical Laboratory Science Review, Fifth Edition (Robert R. Harr); section 8.11; book question 53; continuous question 438. Topic path: Microbiology/Apply knowledge of life cycles/Parasitology/2.
